hypothesis: KDP crystals grown at 36°C with aggressive 2.0°C/hour cooling can achieve acceptable purity in a compressed 5-minute pilot run, validating whether the high-cooling-rate regime can be pushed beyond previous attempts (run_002 at 1.5°C/hour, run_003 at 1.8°C/hour) without thermal-shock damage.
context: Pilot run for the high-cooling-rate parameter regime. Previous attempts at faster cooling have all ended in partial failure — run_002 from a hardware fault, run_003 from a 2-3 minute sensor lag that masked a thermal event. This run pushes one notch further (2.0°C/hour, 36°C target) on the hypothesis that sensor-lag mitigations can keep the run on-rails. The compressed duration means each reading is more load-bearing than usual — the agent has less time to recover from any excursion.

stages.name: equilibration
stages.description: Hold at 36°C. Impurity readings up to 25 ppm during this phase are normal and not a reason to intervene.

stages.name: nucleation
stages.description: Aggressive 2.0°C/hour cooling. Crystal lattice is fragile in this phase — at this cooling rate, the temperature probe lags actual solution temperature by 2-3 minutes (see run_003). Treat fast impurity rate-of-change (>5 ppm/min) as a leading thermal indicator. Do not wait for the temperature reading to confirm.

stages.name: growth
stages.description: Final cooling and crystal maturation. Monitor for delayed dissolution effects from the aggressive cooling phase.

temperature_c.concern: At 2.0°C/hour, the temperature probe lags actual solution temperature by 2-3 minutes. Trust impurity rate-of-change as a leading indicator; treat temperature reading as confirmatory.

impurity_ppm.concern: Impurity rising faster than 5 ppm per minute is a thermal warning sign regardless of what the temperature reading shows. If pH is stable, cause is almost certainly thermal — raise setpoint by 0.5°C preemptively rather than waiting for temperature confirmation. Counterintuitive but necessary at this cooling rate.

ph.concern: Check pH stability before attributing impurity spikes to thermal causes. If pH and impurity rise together, suspect contamination, not thermal stress. Slow monotonic pH drift over multiple hours (see run_004) is a distinct failure mode — watch the trend, not just individual readings.

temperature_high.note: At this cooling rate, never reduce setpoint by more than 0.5°C in a single step. Run_003 showed that a -1.0°C reduction during an active thermal event caused secondary shock. Prefer small corrections.

impurity_rising_without_temp_change.note: Counterintuitive thermal intervention from run_003. If impurity is climbing fast and temperature reading is still nominal, the probe is lagging. Raise setpoint slightly to preempt the dip the probe will report in 2-3 minutes.

contamination_suspected.note: Only intervene chemically if pH is moving alongside impurity. Pure thermal events show impurity change with stable pH.

success_criteria.target: no setpoint change > 0.5°C, no chemical intervention without pH movement

known_risks: Compressed timeline means each reading is high-stakes. There is no time to recover from a misdiagnosed intervention.
Past runs at lower cooling rates (run_002, run_003) revealed two distinct failure modes: hardware fault and sensor lag. This run pushes faster still.

The temperature probe lag observed at 1.8°C/hour (run_003) is expected to be larger at 2.0°C/hour. Estimated lag: 3-4 minutes. Do not trust the temperature reading as a primary indicator during the cooling phase.
Overcorrection is the dominant failure mode at this cooling rate. Keep all setpoint changes small (≤0.5°C) even when readings look alarming.
